Oswiecim New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Oświęcim, Poland

Not demolished. Oświęcim's Jewish community, first documented in 1549, reached 4,950 people (about 40.6 percent of the town) by 1921. In 1940, the Germans established Auschwitz-Birkenau in the town, murdering over 1.1 million people there, including about 1 million Jews. This, the second of Oświęcim's Jewish cemeteries, founded around 1784, holds the graves of Mosze Jakow Scharf, rabbi of Oświęcim and Zator (died 1869); Jakób Haberfeld, community president and vodka and liqueur factory owner (died 1904); and Dow Berisz Frommer, a rabbi and student of Rebbe Szmuel Szmelke Horowic of Nikolsburg (died 1938). In 1941, the Germans established a forced labor camp directly within the cemetery, building barracks, water tanks, and air-raid shelters there, and using tombstones to pave streets. The last person buried in the cemetery was Szymon Kluger, who died in 2000.
